title: Complement of Base 10 Integer
prompt: The complement of an integer is the integer you get when you flip all its bits in binary (0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0), using only the bits needed to represent it (no leading zero bits beyond its own binary length). Given an integer `n`, return its complement.

examples.explanation: 5 is 101 in binary. Flipping every bit gives 010, which is 2.
7 is 111 in binary. Flipping every bit gives 000, which is 0.
10 is 1010 in binary. Flipping every bit gives 0101, which is 5.

hints: Flipping bits is easy with XOR against all 1s, but you must only flip the bits n actually uses — not a fixed 32-bit width.
First figure out how many bits n occupies, then build a mask of that many 1 bits.
XOR n with a mask of the form (2^k - 1), where k is the number of bits in n's binary representation, to flip exactly those bits.

solution.approach: Determine the bit length k of n (the position of its highest set bit plus one). Build a mask consisting of k ones, i.e. (1 << k) - 1. XORing n with this mask flips every bit within n's actual bit-width, which is exactly the complement, while leaving no extra flipped bits beyond n's own length. Special-case n = 0, whose complement is defined as 1.
